1.pericope_label: The worldly sanctuary and its outer room

schools.summary: Chrysostom takes the fashion of the tabernacle as the fourth proof that the old dispensation must end, reading the holy place as the former period and the Holy of Holies as Heaven, entered through the veil of Christ's flesh, and pressing the past tense to show the covenant was already obsolete while it still stood.

Gill states the chapter's design, that Christ's pre-eminence is proved from the tabernacle as it was from priesthood and covenant, and glosses ordinances as righteousnesses appointed by a righteous God. Calvin argues at length that tabernacle is a copyist's insertion, and holds the sanctuary earthly in itself yet heavenly in what it signified, declining any refined explanation of its parts.

Henry reads the sanctuary as wholly of this world in its materials and destined to be taken down, and allegorises its furniture without restraint, the windowless room proving the darkness of that dispensation and the table set opposite the candlestick teaching that communion comes only by light from Christ.

Clarke defends the omission of tabernacle from the text on manuscript evidence, but stands alone in taking worldly as a term of praise meaning adorned and splendid, and supplies the practical detail of the lamps, incense and loaves. Wesley reads candlestick and bread as types of the light and life dispensed by Christ.

Ellicott and Robertson agree that covenant is the understood noun and that worldly marks the sanctuary as belonging to this world in contrast with the heavenly things, Robertson adding that the adjective is predicate rather than attributive. Barnes describes the two rooms but pointedly declines to assign a typical meaning to any article of furniture.

debates: Whether 'worldly' disparages the sanctuary as earthly and carnal (Ellicott, Calvin, Robertson, Henry) or praises it as adorned and splendid (Clarke)
How far the furniture of the holy place may be allegorised: freely (Henry, Wesley) or not at all, since the writer himself declines to (Barnes, Calvin)
outliers: Clarke alone reads the adjective rendered 'worldly' as meaning beautiful and elegant rather than earthly, appealing to Pliny's account of why the Greeks called the universe by that name

3.pericope_label: Behind the veil: censer, ark and cherubim

schools.summary: Gill argues from the second temple that there were indeed two veils in the apostle's day, identifies the censer as the golden one reserved for the day of atonement, and collects the Jewish opinions about the cherubim. Calvin commends the writer for cutting short such refinements, warning that to philosophise past the limits of revelation is useless and dangerous.

Clarke distinguishes the veils by court and sanctuary, and follows Calmet in holding that the description belongs to the Mosaic tabernacle alone, so that discrepancies with Solomon's temple need no reconciling; he closes with a patristic catena of figures for Christ. Wesley takes the censer as the high priest's day-of-atonement vessel and passes on the four-faced reading of the cherubim.

Ellicott and Robertson treat the golden censer as an open question, weighing the Septuagint usage against Philo and Josephus and declining to decide, Robertson noting a manuscript that moves the clause. Barnes defends the censer reading with considerations drawn from custom and safe-keeping, and refuses any speculation about the cherubim as fancy where Scripture is silent.

debates: Whether the golden object is a censer (Gill, Barnes, Wesley) or the altar of incense (the usage of Philo and Josephus, weighed by Ellicott and Robertson, who decline to decide)

What the first veil was: the hanging for the door of the tent (Barnes, Ellicott) or the curtain shutting the holy place off from the court (Clarke), against Gill's appeal to the two veils of the second temple
How far the cherubim may be interpreted: freely (Gill, Wesley, Clarke) or not at all, since Scripture does not explain them (Barnes, Calvin)
outliers: Clarke, following Calmet, denies that the tabernacle and temple accounts need to be harmonised at all, since they describe different buildings

6.pericope_label: The daily service, the yearly entry, and what the Spirit signified by them

schools.summary: Gill counts four entries on the day of atonement and corrects Philo on the penalty, then draws from the naming of the Holy Ghost a chain of doctrine about his personality, deity and authorship of the Levitical types. Calvin makes the closed sanctuary the point of the paragraph, and flatly denies that 'errors' restricts the atonement to sins of ignorance, since every sin involves a blinded judgement.

Henry turns the verse into an obligation on Christian readers, who must not stop at the institutes of the law but learn what the Spirit signified by them, and contrasts the obstructed access of that age with the wider door now opened.

Clarke details the daily ministrations and reads 'errors' strictly as offences committed unawares, made likely by the sheer number of ritual niceties, and notes that the priest's own infirmity required him to share in the sacrifice. Wesley states the same restriction in a sentence and lists the daily offices.

Ellicott explains the present tense as tracing the ordinance of Scripture rather than a still-standing temple, reconciles the Levitical two entries with the Talmud's four, and observes that this Epistle scarcely ever contrasts priests with people. Barnes declines to fix the number of entries and takes 'errors' as widening to fault in general; Robertson notes the lexical distinction between errors and crimes but insists both needed atonement.

debates: Whether 'errors' restricts the day of atonement to sins of ignorance (Clarke, Wesley) or covers sin as such, every sin involving a blinded judgement (Calvin, Barnes, with Robertson allowing the lexical distinction but not the restriction)
How many times the high priest entered the Holy of Holies on the day: two by Leviticus, four by Talmudic tradition (Ellicott, Gill), three or four and immaterial (Barnes, Calvin)
outliers: Ellicott observes that the contrast between the body of priests and the people, central to the Levitical system, is almost absent from this Epistle, which sets one High Priest over against all who approach God through him

9.pericope_label: A parable of the present time, and the coming of the true High Priest

schools.summary: Gill reads 'figure' as a dark saying and argues the phrase means a figure lasting until Christ came, then lists the historical proofs that he has come. Calvin glosses the word by a portrait that recalls the man himself, marks the contrast of flesh and conscience, hears Jeremiah's new covenant behind the time of reformation, and holds that Christ entered heaven through the temple of his own body.
Henry rests all good things past, present and to come on the priestly office of Christ, from which they come to us.

Clarke calls the tabernacle a dark enigmatical representation, insists that even the best worshipper was left with a guilty conscience, protests against the degrading sense commonly given to the word 'carnal', and expounds the time of reformation as the setting straight of everything. Wesley reduces that clause to 'till Christ came' and identifies the greater tabernacle with Christ's own body.

Barnes distinguishes parable from type and warns that safety in interpretation lies in following the inspired writers rather than spiritualising every arrangement. Ellicott and Robertson agree that the better text makes 'carnal ordinances' describe the sacrifices themselves; Robertson calls the failure to cleanse the conscience the real defect of animal sacrifice, notes the medical sense of 'reformation', and identifies the greater tabernacle with heaven.

Cyril cites the passage entire in a catechetical lecture on the garden of the crucifixion, using it to seal the cry 'It is finished': the mystery is fulfilled, what was written is accomplished, and sins are forgiven.

debates: What the greater and more perfect tabernacle is: the body of Christ (Wesley), heaven itself (Robertson), or heaven entered through the temple of his body (Calvin)

Whether the clause means a figure for the time then present or a figure lasting until the present time (Gill), and whether the following relative refers to the parable or to the time (Ellicott, Robertson, Clarke on the variant)
outliers: Clarke protests that 'carnal' here means only what pertains to the body, and is scarcely ever used in the New Testament in the degrading sense that preachers commonly give it
Barnes limits typological interpretation to what the inspired writers themselves explain, comparing the interpreter who leaves those pilots to a ship driven on the open sea

12.pericope_label: His own blood: eternal redemption and a purged conscience

schools.summary: Gill denies Christ any place in Aaron's order and holds those sacrifices no longer acceptable. Calvin forces the alternative that Christ's blood is either better than beasts' blood or worthless, protests that reading 'purifying of the flesh' as a merely civil benefit is heathenish, since the sacraments truly cleansed in a sacramental manner, and refers the eternal Spirit to the Holy Spirit, whose power makes a human death an eternal expiation.

Clarke stresses the once-for-all against the annual entry and defines eternal redemption as a ransom price permanently valid; on the eternal Spirit he declines to choose between the Holy Ghost and the indwelling Deity, holding the two inseparable. Wesley takes the heifer's ashes as restoring men to temple and congregation, refers the eternal Spirit to the work of the whole Trinity, and reads dead works as the works of the devil springing from spiritual death.

Robertson makes Christ both victim and priest and insists the eternal Spirit is Christ's own, giving his blood a moral quality no other sacrifice had. Barnes ranks the differences between the two offerings and catalogues the four opinions on the disputed phrase. Ellicott describes the rite of the red heifer in detail and argues from usage that the Holy Spirit cannot be meant.

debates: What 'the eternal Spirit' denotes: the Holy Spirit (Calvin, Wesley, and the older divines listed by Barnes), Christ's own divine nature or spirit (Ellicott, Robertson), or endless life as opposed to perishable victims (the view Barnes reports from Grotius)

Whether the 'purifying of the flesh' was a merely legal and civil benefit removing disabilities (Clarke, Wesley) or a genuinely sacramental cleansing that pointed to and conveyed a spiritual promise (Calvin)
outliers: Barnes reads the ashes of the heifer as a standing sacrifice kept ready for use, a provision of convenience that spared the expense and delay of a fresh offering at every defilement

15.pericope_label: Mediator of a new covenant, and the death that redeems past transgressions

schools.summary: Chrysostom takes the word as testament and makes the death itself the ground of confidence, since a testament takes force only when its maker has died; he then works the analogy out through heirs and disinherited, obligations laid on the legatees, and the witnesses Christ names for himself.

Gill refers the clause both backward to the purged conscience and forward to the inheritance. Calvin denies that the title of Mediator can be shared, since Christ alone entered the office through death, and presses the retrospective effect of that death against a law whose own remedies left the worshipper in perpetual anxiety.

Henry defines a covenant as an agreement between parties about things in their power and a testament as the deed of one person taking effect at his death, and so reads the gospel as Christ's last will; he names the two ends of the mediation, redemption from transgression and qualification of the called for the inheritance.

Clarke argues that the translators should have kept covenant here as almost everywhere else, explains the mediator's part from the old rite of witnessing and sprinkling, and holds that the death had respect to all time before as well as after it. Wesley renders covenant and makes the article of Christ's death the divide between the old and the new.

Barnes settles the rendering with the observation that a will needs no mediator, and explains how earlier worshippers were saved by offering insufficient blood in faith. Ellicott insists on covenant from the argument of the preceding chapter and distinguishes ransom from sin offering within the single death. Robertson finds here a definite statement that the types drew their worth from the cross.

debates: Whether the word should be rendered covenant (Clarke, Ellicott, Barnes, Robertson, Wesley) or testament (Chrysostom, Henry), Barnes pressing that a will needs no mediator while Chrysostom builds his whole reading on the testator's death
Whether the Mediator's office is unique by nature or only pre-eminent, Calvin denying that any other may remain a mediator alongside Christ
outliers: Clarke identifies 'they which are called' with the Gentiles, given by the new covenant an equal right with the Jews to an inheritance not of land but eternal
Ellicott separates two aspects of the one death, ransom where the debt is penalty and sin offering where debt and payment become sin and punishment

16.pericope_label: Testament or covenant: the death that puts the disposition in force

schools.summary: Gill accepts the will without hesitation and expounds the covenant of grace as a testament with legacies, witnesses and seals. Calvin argues that the verse proves the Epistle was written in Greek and not Hebrew, allows the allusion to the secondary sense, but insists the argument rests on the thing itself, the old covenant having been ratified by blood and so bearing a likeness to a will.

Clarke prints a friend's rendering in which the disputed participle denotes the appointed victim rather than a testator, and urges that testament and testator be forgotten as totally changing the sense. Wesley refuses the wordplay as beneath the apostle's dignity and frankly calls the second verse a very perplexed passage that no current rendering translates literally.

Ellicott sets out both cases fully and decides for covenant, since the alternative makes these two verses the one exception in the New Testament. Barnes supports him by counting the occurrences in the New Testament and the Septuagint, and answers the objection that the word for dead can only mean dead men. Robertson holds the double sense deliberate and both renderings pertinent.

debates: Whether the word here shifts to 'will' (Gill, and the majority Ellicott reports) or keeps the sense 'covenant' throughout, the death being that of the appointed victim (Clarke, Barnes, Ellicott, Calvin), with Robertson taking the ambiguity as intended
Whether the phrase 'over the dead' can be used of slain animals at all, urged as decisive for 'will' and answered by Barnes from the Epistle's own use of the word for dead works
outliers: Wesley declines to let the argument turn on a pun, saying it seems beneath the dignity of the apostle, and admits outright that the passage is perplexed and no current rendering literal

18.pericope_label: The first covenant dedicated with blood: book, people, tabernacle and vessels

schools.summary: Calvin holds that the argument turns on the fact and not on the word, illustrating from the way God's covenant might be called a testimony without impropriety, and makes the recital of the precepts essential, since a sign is an appendage to the word and sacraments are perverted where the commandment goes unexplained. Gill insists the law Moses spoke was the written law and not the rabbis' oral law, and appeals with the others to Josephus for the sprinkling of the tabernacle.

Clarke construes the syntax so that the book was carried and not sprinkled, describes the rite in detail down to the basins and the scarlet thread, finds our Lord's words at the supper deliberately echoing Moses, and draws the lesson that nothing a sinner handles is acceptable without the sprinkling of atoning blood. Wesley refers the missing details to other parts of Moses and suggests the water may typify the blood and water from the pierced side.

Barnes takes this verse as decisive against the reading 'will', since a testator's death is no reason why a covenant should be ratified in blood, and argues that the writer drew the extra details from tradition rather than fresh revelation, which would have spoiled an argument resting on admitted facts; he also presses the verb 'enjoined' as excluding a compact between equals. Ellicott supplies the particulars from elsewhere in the Pentateuch and explains their purpose; Robertson notes the free use made of the old narrative.

Cyril uses the verse in a catechetical argument that grace is given through water, tracing water through creation, the flood, the sea and Sinai, and finding in the water, scarlet wool and hyssop of this passage a proof that where a covenant is made with anyone there is water also.

debates: Whether the book of the covenant was itself sprinkled: Clarke construes the Greek so that it was only carried, while Robertson allows that Exodus is silent but the thing may well have been done

How the writer knew details absent from Exodus: by tradition, since fresh revelation would have undermined an argument resting on what the Hebrews already granted (Barnes), or simply from other passages of Moses (Wesley, Ellicott)
outliers: Barnes argues from the word 'enjoined' that the transaction is not a compact at all, since one party to an agreement does not command the other, and God never gives up his right to enjoin

22.pericope_label: No remission without blood, and a sanctuary not made with hands

schools.summary: Gill reports and rejects a construction that would weaken 'purged' rather than 'all things'. Calvin refuses to allow the exceptions any independence, since water drew its cleansing power from the sacrifices and the purgation reached all though few were sprinkled; he denies that the heavenly things are things in the sky, making the tabernacle a figure of Christ's whole kingdom on earth and above, and rejects Chrysostom's account of the word 'almost'.

Henry identifies the heavenly things with the privileges of the gospel state, begun in grace and perfected in glory, and observes that the earthly sanctuary is itself a pattern of heaven, communion with God there being a heaven upon earth.

Clarke shows the maxim about blood was already rabbinic and explains substitution by the forfeited life, sets out three opinions about what the heavenly things are, and holds that Christ in his crucified body before the throne continues in the constant act of being offered. Wesley reads the heavenly things as our heaven-born spirits while frankly admitting how little is yet known, and explains the plural 'sacrifices' as gathering up all the legal offerings into one.

Ellicott construes the qualifying adverb as governing the whole rule, notes the poor man's flour offering as an exception, and argues that the heavenly things are undefiled but must be brought into association with the one sacrifice before man can enter; he also contrasts the high priest's fearful haste with the manifestation before God's face. Barnes extends the maxim about blood beyond the Levitical system and notes that Jesus never entered the temple proper. Robertson admits the dedication of heaven seems strained and the picture mystical.

Chrysostom explains why the point had to be made at all, describing the pride the Jews took in the temple for its costliness, its beauty and its uniqueness, drawing pilgrims from Babylon to Ethiopia, so that the writer sets the whole heaven against it as he had set Christ's death against the sacrifices.

debates: What the 'heavenly things' are that needed cleansing: heaven itself made accessible (Barnes, Ellicott), the body of Christ or the Church (opinions reported by Clarke), the kingdom of Christ on earth and above (Calvin), or our heaven-born spirits (Wesley), with Robertson admitting the whole conception is strained

Whether the exceptions to cleansing by blood are real, Calvin holding that water and fire drew their efficacy from the sacrifices while Gill, Barnes, Ellicott and Wesley allow them as genuine exceptions
outliers: Calvin names Chrysostom and rejects his account of the word 'almost', which took it to mark the unfitness of merely figurative rites, as inconsistent with the apostle's design
Barnes observes that Jesus, of the tribe of Judah, never entered the temple proper in his life, having no more access than any other Jew

25.pericope_label: Once offered, once to die, and the second appearing apart from sin

schools.summary: Gill reads the single offering as proof of a finished satisfaction and names both those who make Christ offer himself in heaven now and those who offer his body daily; he grounds death in God's decree rather than nature, and denies that Christ bore the sins of all, since all are not justified. Calvin defends a priesthood that need not keep sacrificing, refuses to press 'the foundation of the world' literally, restricts the law of dying once to the ordinary lot, and reads 'many' as set over against 'one' rather than as a measure of extent.

Clarke holds that the crucified body remains a meritorious sacrifice before the throne, takes the putting away of sin as the abolition of the sin offerings and the Mosaic economy, and closes with a prayer for the Lord's coming. Wesley makes the sacrifice the midpoint dividing the world's whole duration, takes 'many' as all who are born, and carefully denies that Scripture teaches a particular judgment immediately after death.

Ellicott identifies the offering with the presentation of blood within the veil and displays the point-by-point parallel between the last two verses. Barnes grounds the single sacrifice in the oneness of death, judgement and probation, and insists that death comes by appointment rather than as a debt of nature. Robertson explains the unreal condition, distinguishes sin as a principle from particular transgressions, and notes that the second appearing is apart from sin and offers no second chance.
Cyril, expounding the manifestation, insists that appearing at the end of the ages is no beginning of being, since the goings forth of the one manifested are from the days of eternity.

debates: For whom Christ bore sins: not for all, since all are not justified (Gill); for as many as are born into the world (Wesley); or a question the text does not raise, 'many' being opposed to 'one' rather than to 'all' (Calvin)
What 'to put away sin' means: to abolish the sin offerings and end the Mosaic economy (Clarke) or to deal with sin itself, in its punishment and its stain (Barnes, Robertson)
Whether anything of the offering continues now: Gill condemns the notion that Christ offers himself in heaven, while Clarke holds the crucified body still a meritorious sacrifice before the throne
outliers: Wesley denies that Scripture anywhere teaches a particular judgment immediately after death, while holding that every man's final state is fixed at the moment of dying

Calvin calls the phrase 'since the foundation of the world' a popular way of speaking, intelligible to common readers though not suitable to over-nice and hair-splitting critics, since sin entered a world already founded
